The Helan Mountains, sometimes called a "mountain island in the sky," form a barrier between the semi-arid Ordos Plateau and Yellow River Valley and the arid desert regions of the Alxa Plateau to the west. Like the mountain ranges in western North America's Great Basin, the Helan Range isolates dense conifer forests and perhaps unique, endemic communities of flora and fauna. Although the ecoregion has received insufficient scientific attention, several rare species are known from the area, including blue sheep, blue-eared pheasants, and the endemic Helan pika. Commercial logging is still a threat to the region's high biological diversity, and habitat destruction continues.

UPO-06: PrhI gene synthesis UPO-06 contains the coding sequence of Ralstonia solanacearum prhI, an ECF sigma factor that is essential for transcription driven by the Prh signal transduction system. This gene is activated by PrhR and subsequently directs sigma factor expression by activating the PprhJ promoter. This sequence is optimized for expression in Escherichia coli. The alitrunk, as illustrated in Fig. 15, is conspicuously swollen and is situated at a much higher level than the propodeal dorsum. The propodeum is armed with a pair of strong spines which are straight to slightly upcurved. The metanotal groove is absent, the metapleural lobes are triangular and conspicuous. The petiole, in profile, has an elongate peduncle and a well developed node, the dorsum of which slopes down posteriorly so that the posterior face is short. The anterior and dorsal surfaces of the postpetiole form a single convexity, the posterior face is truncated. In dorsal view the nodes of both petiole and postpetiole are broader than long. The dorsum of the head is strongly longitudinally rugose, with 5-7 rugae between the frontal carinae at eye-level. The rugae are irregular and tend to meander slightly, with a few anastomoses usually present. The scrobal area is largely smooth but usually has 1-2 fine rugulae traversing its width just behind the antennal fossa. The sides of the head, behind the eyes, are finely reticulate-rugose, a sculpture which extends around the posterior margins of the scrobe to the occiput. All spaces between the rugae are unsculptured or at most bear the faintest superficial traces. The dorsal alitrunk is everywhere finely but strongly reticulate-rugose, with broad, shining interspaces. The petiole dorsum is rugulose, the postpetiole varying from rugulose to only faintly sculptured. The gaster is unsculptured. All dorsal surfaces of head and body are densely clothed with fine acute hairs. Colour dark reddish brown to blackish brown.

However, Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs) cannot substantiate carbon neutrality claims for electrical use beyond a claimant's metered consumption, as the majority of RECs derive from projects that were financially viable without their sale. [10] Consequently, they lack the essential attribute of additionality. Additionality evaluates the counterfactual: what would have occurred under the status quo had the REC not been purchased or contracted. While numerous additionality testing frameworks exist, the core inquiry remains whether the project's financial survival depended on REC revenues. Without verified proof of additionality, RECs cannot be equated to genuine emissions offsets.

A time-dependent mild-slope equation is derived on the basis of the formal derivation of Smith & Sprinks (1975). The higher-order dispersion relation for waves over uneven bottom is obtained. Using only linear dispersion for steady waves, the equation (2.12) of Chamberlain & Porter (1995) is recovered, referred to as the Modified Mild-Slope Equation (MMSE). To the leading-order solution, the study shows that the modified curvature terms of the MMSE have significant effects, while the slope square terms are negligible in accordance with the mild-slope assumption. Therefore, all the modified curvature terms neglected in the MSE are retained, leading to the development of a uniform model. A numerical model using the finite element method (FEM) is developed to predict wave scattering by a varying bottom. In general, the uniform model can predict salient features of waves over various sea beds, such as sinusoidal beds and man-made bars. For sinusoidal beds, the results of the uniform model are in closer agreement with experimental data than other established models. For man-made bars, the results of both the MMSE and the uniform model are in closer agreement with experimental data than the results of Kirby (1986). An important result of the FEM model is its application to the transformation of waves over arbitrarily-varying bathymetry.

The world was once a place of reality and myth; the distinction between the two emerged only with the modern science of comparative biology. But the liminal zone where a figure like Buraq resides has not been abolished by science. We need such transitional objects to bridge seemingly divergent realms of empirical knowledge and spiritual experience. Her presence in contemporary culture is a bridge between rationalist taxonomies and the vestigial power of myth. This finds its most forceful expression in the Islamic transport industry, where Buraq, a figure combining piety and speed, recurs as a patron saint. She gives her name to airlines from Libya to Indonesia, bus companies, freight ships, motorcycle taxis, a space camp, an engineering college, and even Pakistan's first drone. The fluidity of Buraq as an aesthetic and linguistic object explains her pliability in commercial use. She presides not just over wings and wheels, but is also used to sell plastic and PVC, heavy metal, and heavy-duty diesel (BURAQ LUBRICANTS), Indian food, and surgical instruments.

When London’s King’s Cross station expanded northwards in the mid-1860s, its tracks cut through St. Pancras Old Church, the city’s oldest Christian worship site. Thomas Hardy, then working as an architect, was assigned the task of clearing the land. Hardy carefully exhumed the dead, arranging their gravestones in a spiral around a central tree. While that tree still stands today, its roots have begun to envelop the stones, making the inscriptions increasingly difficult to read. Elsewhere in the cemetery, monuments mark the resting places of other notable figures, including Mary Wollstonecraft, author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) and mother of Mary Shelley, who wrote Frankenstein (1818). Nearby rises an imposing mausoleum inscribed with the name Sir John Soane, commemorating the collector-architect whose eccentric house remains on Lincoln’s Inn Fields, as documented in the Description of the House and Museum of Sir John Soane (1835).

The myth in the Phaedrus is of a different kind from the others, and has a greater intensity of meaning. It is nearer to the nature of a parable. It is a figure of speech which can no longer be used, or is only begun to be used, in a future state of existence. The description of the conflict of reasons with passion or righteous indignation on the one hand, and of the animal instincts on the other, in the human soul, takes the place of a former existence as well as of a future. The human soul has been following in the train of some god, before birth beheld truth in the form of the universal, and in the present life is recovering her former existence. Whereas in the other myths the future is simply a reflection of the present, here the present is a reflection of the past. This is a more or less artificial distinction, but may be admitted to exist. It is not likely that Plato was aware of it. It is not a distinction which he would have readily admitted, or of which he was in any way conscious. It is a distinction which has been introduced into the subject by ourselves, and is one of the many examples which show that we are not able to make a sharp separation between the past and the future. The question "Where were men before birth?" is as unfamiliar and unnatural to us as the other question "Where will men be after death?" But the two questions are equally influential and widespread. In the Phaedrus, as in the other myths, the "spiritual combat" of this life is a figure of speech, and the majesty and power of the whole passage, especially of the proem to the Phaedrus, which begins "The mind through all her being is immortal," can only be rendered very imperfectly in another language.

Childhood dental caries is the most prevalent disease of childhood, frequently left untreated and detrimentally influencing general health, physical, developmental, social and learning outcomes. As with other health issues, the greatest burden of dental caries is observed in populations with low socio-economic status. Further, a number of diet-related risk factors for dental caries overlap with those contributing to childhood obesity, such as high and frequent consumption of refined carbohydrates (primarily sugars), soft drinks and other sweetened beverages, and low intake of fluoridated water. Given the prevalence of childhood obesity is at concerning levels in most countries, there is an opportunity to develop interventions that address both of these largely preventable conditions through sustainable and equitable solutions. This study prospectively examines the impact of drink choices on child obesity risk and oral health status.

William Cowper was 61 when he wrote his famous ballad. Thirty years earlier, in a fit of depression, Cowper had attempted suicide in a way that defies description. He swallowed a fatal dose of laudanum, drowned himself, stabbed himself with his pen knife (the blade broke), and hung himself with a garter (which snapped just as he lost consciousness). From these depths, Cowper found solace and strength in composing Christian poems and hymns. One of these works gave the English language the enduring phrase "God moves in a mysterious way" — a truth that resonates deeply not only with William Cowper himself but also with the man he immortalized in his poem, old John Gilpin.

Cell motility plays a fundamental role in embryonic development and is important in a wide variety of physiological and pathophysiological processes. When the regulation of cell movement is perturbed, the consequences can be dramatic, ranging from developmental defects to metastatic cancers. My research is focused on the fundamental mechanisms that regulate cell movement and shape changes. Directed cell migration requires the dynamic remodeling of the cytoskeleton in response to a diverse set of extracellular signals, including both diffusible and surface-bound cues. We are interested in understanding how cells transduce environmental signals into the mechanical forces that are required for directed movement.

The ecoregion includes the moist deciduous forests that surround the montane rainforests in the northern portion of the Western Ghats range. These moist deciduous forests extend across Maharashtra and Karnataka in western India. The Western Ghats are the western edge of the Deccan Plateau, which was formed by the volcanic eruptions that created the Deccan Traps in the Cretaceous period. The Deccan Plate, which forms the plateau, detached from Gondwana during the Cretaceous period, drifted north, and eventually collided with the northern Eurasian continent. The geological uplift of the Western Ghats subsequently intercepted the southwestern monsoon rains, creating a moisture gradient from the wet windward side of the mountains to the increasingly dry leeward side. The annual rainfall in the ecoregion is 1,500 to 2,000 mm, with a 4 to 5-month dry season. The mean annual temperature in the ecoregion ranges from 24 to 27°C, with maximum temperatures inland that can exceed 40°C.

Human beings develop spoken language within the first few years of life, and hearing impairment can not only prevent the ability to speak but also the ability to understand spoken language. By the time it becomes apparent that a severely hearing-impaired (deaf) child has a hearing deficit, communication problems may have already caused issues within the family and hindered social skills, unless the child is part of a Deaf community where sign language is used instead of spoken language (see Deaf Culture). In many developed countries, evaluations for hearing occur during the newborn period to prevent inadvertent isolation of a deaf child within a hearing family. Although sign language is a full means of communication, literacy ultimately depends on the ability to understand speech; in the vast majority of written language, the sound of the word is coded in symbols. Although an individual who hears well enough to learn to speak and read will retain the ability to read even if their hearing becomes too impaired to hear voices, a person who never heard well enough to learn to speak is rarely able to read proficiently (see [4]). Most evidence suggests that the early identification of hearing impairment is key to ensuring a child with very insensitive hearing learns spoken language effectively. Listening also plays an important role in learning a second language.

Dr. Henry analyzed the composition and investigated the properties of carburetted hydrogen gas. His experiments were numerous and accurate, and were made upon a variety of substances; and having obtained the gas from wood, peat, different kinds of coal, oil, wax, &c. he minutely examined and considered the various quantities of light, and the different quantities of heat, produced by burning it.

In the Revolution, the French throne met with a new one, and was shattered. The people, in the midst of their dreams of equality, lost their own hands. The large and soft arm-chairs, the full and ample draperies, the cushions of eider down, all the other delicacies which we alone understood of all the European family, led only to the imprisonment of their possessors; and if you had the misfortune to inhabit a spacious hotel, within a court, to avoid the odious noise and smells of the street, you had your throat cut. That mode of treating elegant manners put them out of fashion; they were speedily abandoned, and the barbarity of their successors still so lingers amongst us, that every day you see put into the lumber-room an elegant Grecian chair which has broken your arm, and canopies which smell of the stable, because they are stuffed with hay.

All of de Sève’s illustrations are equipped with identifying captions except one, listed simply as l’animal anonyme (the unidentified animal). Most later naturalists agreed that it must be meant to represent a fennec fox, though some have also suggested a bat-eared fox. Whatever the case may be, one thing is certain: de Sève loved drawing large ears. With their strangely human faces and richness of setting, De Sève’s wonderful illustrations, engraved for publication in the Histoire by Louis Le Grand, are a true treasure of eighteenth-century naturalism. In the nervous system, transduction is the conversion of stimuli into electrical impulses. In sensory transduction, physical or chemical stimuli are converted into electrical impulses by sensory receptors. For example, in the visual system, rod and cone cells in the retina convert physical stimuli into signals that can travel to the brain. When light strikes the photoreceptor cells in the retina, it causes a conformational change in a protein called rhodopsin. This conformational change sets off a cascade of events that leads to a change in the electrochemical gradient of the photoreceptor. This decrease in the electrochemical gradient causes a decrease in the electrical signals being sent to the brain. Thus, in this example, more light hitting the photoreceptor results in fewer electrical impulses being sent to the brain.

The total volume of lung tissue was computed as the volume of lung tissue = number of voxels × volume of the voxel provided that the compartment considered has a CT number above zero. The change in functional residual capacity resulting from PEEP withdrawal (ΔFRC) was computed as the difference in total gas volume in the whole lung between PEEP and ZEEP states. Alveolar derecruitment was defined as the difference in gas volume within poorly aerated and nonaerated lung regions between PEEP and ZEEP states. The changes in gas volume from PEEP withdrawal in normally aerated lung regions, characterized by CT attenuations between -500 and -900 HU (see Figure 2), were also computed. Mobile internet expands the immersive potential of storytelling by introducing electronic games powered by portable, location-aware interfaces. In doing so, this latest iteration of electronic games empowers the player not only as an avatar in a gameworld but also as a co-author alongside original designers. Location-aware interfaces allow players to implicate places in the physical world as part of their gameworld and vice versa, a first for interactive media. Beyond empowering the player in worldmaking, mobile games eschew linear narratives in favor of cooperative storytelling reliant on the player's experience of place. While this author-player worldmaking concept is not new, mobile games evolve the process beyond the constraints of traditional video games. By extending the worldmaking process beyond the screen and into the physical world, location-aware interfaces co-opt the player's sensory experiences of real-world places as storytelling tools. In this essay, we theorize the unique storytelling potential of mobile games while describing our experience attempting to harness this potential through the design and implementation of our hybrid-reality game, University of Death.

The Ruhr Area (German: Ruhrgebiet), also called simply Ruhr, is an urban area in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, consisting of a number of large former industrial cities bordered by the rivers Ruhr to the south, Rhine to the west, and Lippe to the north. Southwest it borders the Bergisches Land. It is considered part of the larger Rhine-Ruhr metropolitan area of more than 12 million people, among the largest in Europe. The cities of the area include (from west to east) Duisburg, Oberhausen, Bottrop, Mülheim an der Ruhr, Essen, Gelsenkirchen, Bochum, Herne, Hamm, Hagen, and Dortmund as well as parts of the more "rural" districts of Wesel, Recklinghausen, Unna and Ennepe-Ruhr. These cities have, in fact, grown together into a large complex with a huge population of about 5 million, making it the fifth largest urban area in Europe after Moscow, Greater London, Paris, and Istanbul. The Ruhr area is by far the most unpleasant part of Germany from the hitchhiking perspective. It has a very high density of motorways but it is quite difficult to get out of the region as there are many minor roads which make it difficult to find a good place to hitch. Germany is in general a nice place to hitch, but you should stay on the main motorways in the Ruhr Area (A1, A2, A3) since the smaller roads are really difficult to hitch. There is very little transit traffic in the Ruhr Area. Hitching inside the Ruhr Area is comparable to hitching in a big city like Istanbul; the cities are independent, but for a traveler they all seem like districts of one big city.
